title: How to Build a Bedtime Reading Routine Your Child Loves
excerpt: A calm bedtime reading routine can take 20 minutes. Here is how to start, what to read, and how to keep it going as kids grow.
body:
Pick the same calm time each night, switch off screens, and read together for about 15 to 20 minutes. Let your child choose the book. A steady routine beats a perfect one, and it can keep going long after your child learns to read alone.

Why does a bedtime reading routine help?

Bedtime is a natural time to slow down. A research review on bedtime routines in young children found that consistent routines are linked to better sleep. They're also linked to stronger language, early literacy and emotional regulation. In that review, routines that included reading were linked to longer sleep in toddlers, and language-based routines at age 3 were linked to higher vocabulary at age 5. (Mindell and Williamson, Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2017)

One honest note. The same review mentions a study where sharing books at bedtime didn't change how well kids slept. So think of reading as a calm, close way to end the day, not a sleep cure. Scholastic's parent team describes bedtime reading as soothing, and says most parents already read to their kids before sleep. (Scholastic Parents)

How long should bedtime reading take?

About 20 minutes is a good target. Scholastic suggests setting aside 20 minutes in the evening. First Things First says even a few minutes a night helps build vocabulary and school readiness. (First Things First)

Keep an eye on the whole routine, too. The research review warns that a bedtime routine running longer than 30 to 40 minutes may work against sleep. So if bath, teeth and pajamas already take 15 minutes, aim for 10 to 15 minutes of reading. A short session that ends while your child still wants more is a win.

What does a simple routine look like?

Keep the order the same every night. The American Academy of Pediatrics promotes an easy three-step version of this called Brush, Book, Bed, developed with its early-literacy partner Reach Out and Read: brush teeth, read a book, then lights out. Easy to remember, even at the end of a long day. (HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics)

Three small habits help it stick:

  • Switch screens off before the routine starts, and keep the lights low. The research review lists TV and electronics at bedtime as unhelpful.
  • Read in the same cozy spot each night, like the bed or a corner of the couch.
  • Tie it to something fun. Scholastic suggests reading during bath or tooth-brushing time to make those tasks more enjoyable.

What should we read?

Let your child choose. For ages 3 to 6, Scholastic notes that short books of about 40 pages or fewer can be finished in one sitting, which is handy on busy weeknights. Ask what your child thinks will happen next, and let them point to the words as you read.

For ages 7 and up, try a chapter book across several nights. Stopping at an exciting spot gives your child a reason to look forward to tomorrow. Common Sense Media encourages reading aloud to big kids, picking books that match their interests, and trying different genres. It also cites literacy author Jim Trelease's view that listening level stays ahead of reading level until about eighth grade. (Common Sense Media)

How do I keep it going as my child grows?

Don't stop when your child can read alone. Common Sense Media says reading aloud still builds reading and listening skills after age 5. Try taking turns, with you reading one page and your child the next. Or sit side by side, each with your own book. Scholastic notes that reading alone in the same room still counts as shared time.

Miss a night? No big deal. Pick it up tomorrow. A routine grows from lots of ordinary evenings, not a perfect streak.

Can a story about my child make bedtime reading special?

It can add a little magic. Lots of kids love hearing their own name in a story. At Growing Minds, we make personalized illustrated chapter books where your child is the hero, built around something they're working on right now, like starting school or managing big feelings. A 30-chapter story gives your bedtime routine something to look forward to, night after night.

We can't promise any one book will change sleep or reading habits. But a story that's clearly about them is a good reason to hear, "One more chapter?"

Frequently asked questions

What age should we start a bedtime reading routine? Any age works. The research review above focuses on children from birth to age 5, but reading aloud keeps helping older kids too.

How many minutes should we read each night? About 15 to 20 minutes is a good goal, and even a few minutes counts. Try to keep the whole bedtime routine under roughly 30 to 40 minutes.

Are screens okay as part of bedtime? It's better to turn them off. First Things First suggests switching screens off and keeping lights low, and the research review lists TV and electronics at bedtime as unhelpful.

What if we miss a night? Just start again the next evening. A steady routine is built over lots of nights, not one perfect week.

Should I keep reading aloud once my child can read alone? Yes, if your child enjoys it. Common Sense Media notes that reading aloud still builds reading and listening skills in older kids. Taking turns is a good middle step.

sources.title: Jodi A. Mindell and Ariel A. Williamson, "Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond", Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2017
American Academy of Pediatrics (HealthyChildren.org), "Brush, Book, Bed"
Scholastic Parents Staff, "4 Benefits of Bedtime Reading for Younger Kids", April 2022
Common Sense Media editors, "10 Reasons You Should Read Aloud to Big Kids, Too", updated July 2025
First Things First, "Three simple steps for a better bedtime routine"
